title: Checkpoint: Waves and Tides
objective: After this level you can explain what makes waves and tides.
summary: Tides are waves too: very long-period ones, with high tide at the crest. Wind waves, tides and storm surge are three ways the sea rises, each with its own engine.

cards.headline: The longest wave you will ever meet passes your beach twice a day.
cards.body: You've never noticed it, because each one takes a little over 12 hours to go by. Let's meet it, then line up every wave this chapter taught.

cards.fact: Tides are waves too: very long-period ones.
cards.context: NOAA describes tides as waves that move through the ocean, driven by the Moon and Sun. When the crest reaches your coast, that's high tide; the trough brings low tide. Picture Level 24's two bulges as crests. Since most coasts see a high tide a little over every 12 hours, that's how long one of these waves takes to pass.

items.label: Wind waves
points: Wind speed, time and fetch set their size
Swell: crests more than 10 to 12 seconds apart
Break where the water is about 1.3 times their height deep

items.label: Tides
points: Moon and Sun; the Sun's pull a little under half
A crest a little over every 12 hours
Up to 16 m in the Bay of Fundy

items.label: Storm surge
points: A storm's winds push water ashore
Surge plus tide makes the storm tide

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How wind builds waves that carry energy across whole oceans while the water itself mostly stays put.
Why waves slow down, grow taller and break as they reach shallow water.
How the Moon and Sun raise the tides, and why tides are biggest at new and full moon.
Why some bays get giant tides, and how a storm surge rides on top of the tide to flood coasts.

questions.prompt: Waves and tides recap: how does NOAA describe the tides?

options.label: As currents that flow in circles around each ocean
options.rationale: Tides are waves, not circling currents.

options.label: As very long-period waves driven by the Moon and Sun
As wind waves that grow very large
options.rationale: Wind makes waves; the Moon and Sun make tides.

options.label: As changes in sea level caused by rain
options.rationale: Rain has nothing to do with tides.

questions.explanation: NOAA describes tides as very long-period waves that move through the oceans in response to forces from the Moon and Sun.

questions.prompt: Waves and tides recap: if the tide is a wave, what is high tide at your beach?

options.label: The wave breaking on the sand
options.rationale: Tides are far too long to break like surf.

options.label: The wave's trough arriving
The wave's crest arriving
A storm surge passing through
options.rationale: A surge is a storm effect, not the tide.

questions.explanation: When the crest of the tide wave reaches a place, it's high tide; the trough brings low tide.

questions.prompt: Waves and tides recap, from Level 21: a fierce gust blows over open sea for just a few minutes. Why are there no big waves?

options.label: Gusts move only the air, never the water
options.rationale: Wind does make waves; this one just didn't last.

options.label: Big waves need only a long fetch
options.rationale: Fetch alone is not enough either.

options.label: The tide was going out
options.rationale: Tides do not stop wind waves forming.

options.label: It needs speed, time and fetch together

questions.explanation: Large waves form only when strong wind blows for a long time over a long fetch; a few minutes of wind is not enough.

questions.prompt: Waves and tides recap, from Level 22: a 2 m wave heads for shore. About how deep is the water where it breaks?

options.label: About 0.5 m
options.rationale: Too shallow: it breaks well before that.

options.label: About 2.6 m
About 13 m
About 26 m
options.rationale: Far too deep: that wave would still be rolling.

questions.explanation: Waves generally break where the water is about 1.3 times as deep as the wave is tall: 1.3 times 2 m is about 2.6 m.

questions.prompt: Waves and tides recap, from Level 29: what is a storm tide?

options.label: Storm surge plus the normal tide
A tide caused by the Sun during storms
options.rationale: The Sun does not cause the surge.

options.label: Another name for a rogue wave
options.rationale: Rogue waves are single giant waves.

options.label: The lowest tide after a storm
options.rationale: It's the total high water during a storm.

questions.explanation: Storm tide is the total water level during a storm: the storm surge plus the normal astronomical tide.
